stories.topic: Where the light bulb went off: French healthcare
stories.summary: Ajay says the French healthcare system is where the idea clicked for him. France runs an unusually good mix of public and private healthcare, while the US spends about three times as much as other OECD countries and gets worse outcomes. A health enthusiast naturally studies France and asks why India can't adopt it. But the French system rests on about a hundred other French subsystems: budgeting, rule of law, product and medical liability, government HR and contracting, and how the public and private sectors behave. Health specialists, swapping ideas between the NHS and the French system, never look at those parts.
stories.insight: A successful institution is the visible top of a large stack of supporting systems. The specialist's depth is exactly what keeps that stack out of view, so the expert is often the one most likely to propose a transplant that fails.
stories.quote: The mistake around invisible infrastructure would be to start thinking that because XYZ design of the French healthcare system works so well in France, we could or should transplant that into India.

stories.topic: The fruit of the poisonous tree
stories.summary: Ajay describes a US doctrine he believes was set by judges around 1938. Suppose a cop taps your phone without a warrant and finds proof you are the murderer. The court throws all that evidence out, because evidence obtained illegally is inadmissible. Without this bright-line rule, cops would never bother with warrants: if they found something, the ends would justify the means, and if they didn't, they would still have blackmail material. Amit adds a second safeguard: investigation and prosecution are separate departments, and prosecutors are judged on successful prosecutions, so weak cases get filtered out before they reach court. Ajay notes that India has neither protection.
stories.insight: Privacy was protected in the West long before computers existed, through rules that change police incentives. When modern Western debates take state restraint for granted, it is because this invisible infrastructure was built generations ago.
stories.quote: If illegally obtained evidence is permissible in court, why would a cop ever take the permission? They would always go around like a lawless creature.

stories.topic: Lant Pritchett's New York taxi driver
stories.summary: Ajay passes on Lant Pritchett's analogy. Someone with twenty years inside the Norwegian military, the New York Fed or the Bank of England knows as much about policy design as a New York taxi driver knows about how cars work. The driver can steer, brake and read the lights, but knows nothing about why the car was built as it was or what trade-offs shaped its brakes. Practitioners likewise take for granted centuries of institution-building, such as the fact that something like India's Armed Forces Special Powers Act is unimaginable in Norway. Yet Indians often defer to them because they have 'worked twenty years at the Bank of England.'
stories.insight: Running a system and designing one are different kinds of knowledge. Practitioners know the 'how'; the 'why' is about incentives, and only the 'why' carries over to a new country.
stories.quote: They know the how. But they don't know the why. And the why is an incentive story.

stories.summary: Amit names his episode with Sowmya Dhanaraj as one of his top ten on The Seen and the Unseen. She studied under Susan at IGIDR. Her parents worked in a factory, and her mother ran a tea stall on the Coimbatore Highway for many years. Her education was the same as anyone else's, but her thinking rests on lived knowledge of how India actually works, not on frameworks imported from abroad.
stories.insight: Good policy instinct comes from being rooted in a place, not from credentials. Ajay connects this to 'authenticity': if you want to transplant something into Haryana, you need to know whether a truck carrying expensive goods can safely drive at night on a given road there.
stories.quote: She doesn't have that elite education. She doesn't have foreign ideas implanted into her brain. She's seen the world. She's asked the right questions.

stories.topic: Swachh Bharat toilets with no drainage
stories.summary: Amit recalls a point Shruti Rajagopalan made on The Seen and the Unseen. Swachh Bharat built toilets in villages everywhere, but often with no drainage. Higher-caste households would not handle their own waste, so they had lower-caste people do it, which worsened caste practices. Ajay objects that drainage is visible infrastructure: what kind of water and sanitation expert builds a toilet without thinking about water coming in and sewage going out? Amit replies that things like drainage, water and electricity become invisible because we assume they exist.
stories.insight: Every intervention depends on supporting systems. Leave them out and the fix can make the original problem worse.
stories.quote: So it kinda made the problem worse because you didn't handle what I would call the invisible infrastructure of the drainage system.

stories.summary: After the Latur earthquake, Amit recalls, Japan sent about four hundred air conditioners as relief. Most of the affected places had no electricity, and the survivors didn't need air conditioners anyway.
stories.insight: Someone looking from far away, whether a rich donor or an Ivy League policy elite, assumes the infrastructure they live with exists everywhere. Then the 'API call' fails without anyone noticing.
stories.quote: Japan sent some four hundred air conditioners or something as relief. Which makes absolutely no sense, right?

stories.topic: How the show got its name
stories.summary: When Amit and Ajay were choosing a name, they took two candidates from favourite songs: John Lennon's 'Watching the Wheels' and the phrase 'everything is everything' from Bruce Springsteen's 'You're Missing'. Amit picked the second, and Ajay said the song meant a lot to him too. Once they set the songs aside, the phrase still fit because it describes how they try to think about the world.
stories.insight: The name states the episode's argument: no field can be understood on its own terms alone.
stories.quote: And then when we put the songs aside, everything is everything just made sense because that's how we try to think about the world.

recommendations.item: Premature Imitation and India's Flailing State
recommendations.creator: Shruti Rajagopalan and Alexander Tabarrok
recommendations.context: Brought up right after Ajay stated the transplantation problem; Amit calls it 'this great paper' (and almost mangles the title).
recommendations.reason: It makes essentially the same argument as this episode: India copies the forms of advanced-economy policy too early and ends up with a flailing state. It also links to Lant Pritchett's work and the idea of isomorphic mimicry.

recommendations.item: Elite Imitation in Public Policy (Episode 180 of The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Shruti Rajagopalan and Alex Tabarrok
recommendations.context: Amit's episode with the authors of the Premature Imitation paper.
recommendations.reason: A long conversation about why policies that elites copy from abroad fail in India, the closest companion to this episode.

recommendations.creator: Vijay Kelkar and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Ajay draws the 'rocket and payload' analogy from 'the Kelkar and Shah book' in his final point on what is to be done.
recommendations.reason: It explains why the foundations of government (HR, contracting, budgeting, checks on coercive power) matter more than domain expertise, a lens that applies to every government agency.

recommendations.item: Understanding India's Pensions Disaster (Episode 65 of Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Ajay points to 'an EIE episode on pension reforms' while explaining why India's military reforms got stuck on military pensions.
recommendations.reason: It fills in the pensions example: if India had a sound, economy-wide defined-contribution system, the military could simply plug into it.

recommendations.item: The Horrors of KYC (Episode 74 of Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Ajay recalls that the KYC episode covered mass surveillance, just before arguing that India's privacy problem is the state.
recommendations.reason: Background on how the Indian state can see into citizens' lives, which is the privacy battle Ajay says India has to fight first.

recommendations.item: Public Choice Theory Explains SO MUCH (Episode 33 of Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Linked in the show notes; in the episode Ajay calls public choice theory 'a superpower' for finding invisible infrastructure.
recommendations.reason: Assume nobody is a saint and ask what each actor is maximising. Following the incentives leads you to the hidden systems that make an institution work.

recommendations.item: Stay Away From Luxury Beliefs (Episode 46 of Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Amit says that once the state problem in privacy is handled, 'we can get to the luxury beliefs, as it were, later.'
recommendations.reason: About beliefs imported from rich-world discourse that don't address India's actual priorities.

recommendations.item: India's Problem is Poverty, Not Inequality
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Amit complains that 'too many of these foreign educated kids will say inequality, where actually poverty is our problem.'
recommendations.reason: Explains why poverty and inequality are 'two completely different things' and why poverty is India's real problem.

recommendations.item: Ajay Shah Brings the Dreams of the 20th Century (Episode 402 of The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Amit mentions their ten-and-a-half-hour conversation, where he kept riffing on C.L.R. James's 'what do they know of cricket'.
recommendations.reason: A very long version of the breadth-over-specialisation case, applying the 'what do they know of X who only X know' idea across many fields.

recommendations.creator: John Lennon
recommendations.context: One of two favourite songs they considered when naming the show.
recommendations.reason: A song both hosts love; it was the runner-up name for the podcast.

recommendations.creator: Bruce Springsteen
recommendations.context: Amit took the phrase 'everything is everything' from this 'great' Springsteen song, and Ajay said it resonates with him too.
recommendations.reason: The source of the show's name and its worldview.

recommendations.item: Life Lessons From Chess in 2024 (Episode 81 of Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Amit refers back to it while arguing that mastering one subject isn't enough.
recommendations.reason: It argues that renewal matters more than mastery, because experts in narrow fields tend to stop learning.

recommendations.item: Sowmya Dhanaraj Is Making a Difference (Episode 380 of The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Sowmya Dhanaraj
recommendations.context: Amit says it is definitely in his top ten Seen and the Unseen episodes and uses it to introduce 'thinking locally'.
recommendations.reason: An example of policy thinking that starts from lived Indian reality rather than imported frameworks.

recommendations.creator: Johan Norberg
recommendations.context: Amit says he learned about Sweden and Scandinavia from Norberg and tells listeners to 'please check them out.'
recommendations.reason: Norberg shows that Scandinavia grew rich through free markets and entrepreneurship first and added the welfare state only after becoming advanced economies. That order matters for anyone who wants to copy Sweden.

recommendations.item: Economic growth is enough and only economic growth is enough
recommendations.creator: Lant Pritchett with Addison Lewis
recommendations.context: Amit cites 'Lant Pritchett's great paper on the subject' while arguing for growth before welfarism.
recommendations.reason: Amit cites it for a 99% correlation between human welfare indicators and per capita GDP: growth is what raises human welfare.

recommendations.item: Understanding the State (Episode 25 of The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Amit recalls Ajay explaining in episodes 25 and 26 that the state should intervene only when there is a market failure.
recommendations.reason: Lays out the framework for when the state should act. Amit adds that a market failure is necessary for intervention but not sufficient.

recommendations.item: When Should the State Act? (Episode 26 of The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: The companion to episode 25, cited in the same breath.
recommendations.reason: Develops the market-failure test, which supports this episode's case for a small, focused state given India's limited state capability.

recommendations.item: Swachh Bharat (Episode 82 of The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Shruti Rajagopalan
recommendations.context: The source of the toilets-without-drainage example.
recommendations.reason: Shows how a well-intentioned scheme that ignored its supporting infrastructure ended up reinforcing caste practices.

recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Amit mentions it right after Ajay's plug for the show, during the breadth-versus-specialisation discussion.
recommendations.reason: Aimed at what Amit says the education system fails to do: give students breadth and ways into depth.

core_ideas.explanation: A policy or institution that works in one country depends on many surrounding capabilities: courts, rule of law, liability regimes, government HR and contracting, anti-corruption norms. You can't copy the visible part (a Norwegian military doctrine, a French health design, a TSMC) and expect it to work where those supports are missing. The supports are not literally hidden. They are invisible because modern specialists don't look at them.
core_ideas.quote: If you only bother to look, all the things are there. It's not difficult to see the French legal system, the working of the courts, the rule of law, the government HR, the government contracting, the product liability, the healthcare liability, all all those pieces are there. But the thing is that the people who are specialists tend to be blind about them.

core_ideas.explanation: Amit brings in the biological term isomorphic mimicry, and Ajay separates it from the invisible-infrastructure problem. In mimicry, a harmless moth wears a poisonous insect's colours: India sets up a 'central bank' or 'food safety regulator' with all the pomp, staff and conference rooms, but no real people, processes, checks or incentives inside. In the invisible-infrastructure failure, the effort is genuine and the inside is staffed, but the institution still doesn't work because what it depends on is missing. Amit suggests the two sit on a continuum.
core_ideas.quote: Here inside it's not empty, but it's actually malfunctioning. It's not performing as intended.

core_ideas.concept: Every institution makes 'API calls' to the rest of the economy
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay uses a software analogy. Each institution calls on capabilities it doesn't own. A military calls 'pensions'; a hospital calls 'product liability' and 'courts'. In rich countries those calls return reliably. Underdevelopment means the capability is missing or unreliable. India's military reforms stalled because military pensions were never fixed as part of an economy-wide pension reform. Courts work the same way: the key measure of a legal system is the chance a case is decided correctly. Ajay guesses about 80% for a UK malpractice case and near a coin toss in India, and that difference changes how the whole healthcare system behaves.
core_ideas.quote: So think of that as an API call that each piece of the policy ecosystem requires other pieces to work.

core_ideas.concept: Incentives and checks and balances usually come from outside the institution
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay's second and third lenses. People inside an institution are self-interested, and their incentives are shaped by the surrounding culture. A canteen vendor in the Norwegian military can't even imagine corruption in food procurement, but Indian conditions are different, and that changes how the whole organisation behaves. Many checks are also inherited rather than designed. The US Inspector General system, built over a hundred years, gives every federal agency a reasonably independent corruption investigator, and new agencies simply assume they will have one.
core_ideas.quote: Okay, this just works. It was developed over a hundred years. And uh today when you are developing a new federal agency in America, you just take this for granted.

core_ideas.concept: Public choice theory as a superpower for seeing what's hidden
core_ideas.explanation: Don't assume the Norwegian general or the French doctor is a good person. Ask awkward questions. Why won't the doctor overprescribe for a kickback from the X-ray clinic? Why won't the general take a cut on procurement? Why will a soldier stand and fight instead of running? Ajay says the honest answers almost always lead to the invisible infrastructure.
core_ideas.quote: Don't say nobility, patriotism, those are all bad reasons. Think deeply about incentives. Why do people behave the way they behave, and that will take you to the invisible infrastructure.

core_ideas.concept: India's privacy fight is against the state, not Google
core_ideas.explanation: After WWII, Germany and other OECD countries built checks so that even an elected Hitler could not harm citizens. Add the fruit of the poisonous tree doctrine and the separation of powers, and Western privacy debates can assume the state is restrained, which is why they focus on Google and targeted ads. Indian policy people who learned privacy from Western blogs and the GDPR carried that focus into India and sent the debate in the wrong direction. In India the danger is a state that can see everything about citizens without checks.
core_ideas.quote: In the Indian context, there is only one problem to solve. How to shut down state access to information about the people. We'll get to the private sector, you know, much later.

core_ideas.concept: Be wary of specialisation: breadth is the harder, more useful skill
core_ideas.explanation: The modern world rewards narrow expertise, because expertise earns respect. Ajay argues narrow depth makes you less useful and is the easier path. Build broad understanding, plus the ability to go deep on anything within a couple of weeks when needed. Amit generalises C.L.R. James: 'what do they know of X who only X know'. He adds that more than mastery, people need renewal, because narrow masters stop learning.
core_ideas.quote: And when all you have is a five watt bulb, you want to focus it on one square micron. So you'll pick a tiny piece of the universe and you will gain mastery. You will know everything about nothing.

core_ideas.concept: STEM is easy, humanities is hard
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay says he and a colleague once silently agreed on this. Technical knowledge comes from a finite set of books, can be taught, and can be examined; an LLM can quiz you on matrix differentiation. Understanding the world has no syllabus or exam. Amit adds that by 'humanities' they mean learning about the human condition through books, world cinema, music and engaging with life, not today's university departments.
core_ideas.quote: Imagine you can run an exam to know that you know how to solve quadratic equations. What exam is going to test that you understand epistemology?

core_ideas.explanation: Narrow depth makes you a technician, a useful part of a machine that people get work out of. Thinking at a larger scale, including strategy and entrepreneurship, takes breadth. Organisations prefer people who 'shut up and execute' and use strong narrow incentives to keep them that way. That suits the principal, not necessarily the agent. Amit adds that the over-specialised risk being replaced by AI. Like Henry Ford imagining cars when others wanted faster horses, the aim is to think one level above your specialty.
core_ideas.quote: So for each of us as we grow into life, the very essence of growing is developing breadth, is developing strategic sense, is rising from being a technician to being a thinker.

core_ideas.explanation: Before transplanting the French healthcare system into Haryana, you have to understand Haryana well, down to whether a truck carrying expensive goods can safely travel a certain road at night. That kind of common-sense knowledge comes only from being embedded in a place. Ajay also warns Indians who want to export Indian successes to Morocco or Mozambique, whose invisible infrastructure is different again.
core_ideas.quote: You have to be there. the beautiful humanities word authenticity that you are embedded in that culture, in that place.

core_ideas.concept: Sometimes the wise move is to do nothing
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay admires Sweden ('I confess I'm a soft pinko'), but Indian state capability is a finite muscle. It should go to a few problems, and the state should walk away from problems that are too hard or impossible in Indian conditions. His example is that India should not attempt defined-benefit pensions at all; the invisible infrastructure is hostile to them. Amit adds that a market failure is necessary for state intervention but not sufficient. The state should act on things like famines, humanitarian crises and pollution, not on small matters, because India tends to do many things badly instead of a few things well, and every intervention has an opportunity cost.
core_ideas.quote: So many times we should have the courage and clarity to walk away. Many, many times the wise answer is to shrink the scope of the Indian state.

core_ideas.concept: Growth first, welfare state later: the order of operations
core_ideas.explanation: Drawing on Johan Norberg, Amit says Scandinavian countries got rich through free markets and entrepreneurship and built welfare states only afterwards, while keeping business easy. Lant Pritchett's paper shows a 99% correlation between human welfare indicators and per capita GDP. Indians who want a Swedish welfare state now are skipping the growth and the invisible infrastructure that made it affordable.
core_ideas.quote: Get the economic growth first and maybe once we've gotten everybody out of poverty you have the luxury of once the pie is big enough that you can redistribute some of it.

core_ideas.concept: Design the state for the worst person in power
core_ideas.explanation: Amit says the test of state design is how little damage the worst possible ruler could do, and a constitution is central to that. In his view India's constitution fails this test because it centralises too much power, so even good people behave badly with it. Ajay links this back to the episode's theme: the constitution sits at the bottom of every failure of invisible infrastructure.
core_ideas.quote: And every healthcare expert needs to ultimately trace the dots of the malfunctioning invisible infrastructure to the constitution.

core_ideas.concept: Rocket and payload: fix the foundations
core_ideas.explanation: From the Kelkar and Shah book. Take the central statistical organisation. The 'payload' is the domain work: GDP measurement, double deflation. The 'rocket' is most of the organisation: budgeting, public financial management, contracting, HR. If the rocket fails, domain expertise is useless. So more people should work on foundations that cut across sectors, such as rule of law, checks on coercive power, government HR and contracting, and agency governance, because fixing them improves every sector at once.
core_ideas.quote: If we fix government HR all across the landscape, we will get hundreds of better functioning government agencies.

core_ideas.concept: Economic development means more API calls that work
core_ideas.explanation: To build a TSMC in India, list its external interfaces: the public goods it needs from government and the private firms it must contract with. Firms like Infosys work in India because their particular calls return reliably. In this view, development is the steady growth of a country's public-goods capabilities, its private contracting capabilities and its legal system's contract enforcement, which lets more complex firms take root.
core_ideas.quote: So conceptually economic development one by one is about an ever expanding range of the public goods capabilities of the country.

jokes_and_cultural_references.content: Amit's opening: 'Welcome to Everything Is Everything and welcome to the Seen and the Unseen. And no, this is not a crossover episode,' since the episode is all about unseen things.

Amit naming Shruti Rajagopalan and Alex Tabarrok's paper: 'They did this great paper called Premature uh I was about to say ejaculation. That's not the name of the… Premature Imitation and the Flailing State.'

Ajay inverts the old economist joke: 'An economist is someone who, when something works in practice, wonders whether it works in theory. So here you have something that doesn't work in practice, and so we should understand why it doesn't work in theory.'
Amit sums up isomorphic mimicry in Hindi: 'Bahar se central bank, andar se khokhla', meaning a central bank on the outside, hollow on the inside.
Isomorphic mimicry from biology: a harmless moth wears a poisonous insect's colours so birds won't eat it. Ajay applies it to Indian agencies that copy the look of first-world institutions.

Amit uses American cop shows to explain the fruit of the poisonous tree: 'anyone who's watched like a Chicago PD or a law and order would know that… if you get evidence from an illegal search and seizure, it's not admissible.'
Post-1945 Germany: Ajay describes the effort, across the OECD and most of all in Germany, to protect individuals 'even if a Hitler would win a future election a la 1933.'
Lant Pritchett appears twice: his idea of the 'flailing state', and his New York taxi driver analogy for first-world practitioners.

Ajay quotes 'the great man Karl Marx' (the tombstone line about philosophers and changing the world). Amit quickly tells listeners it's tongue-in-cheek and that both think Marx's ideas were devastating: 'Groucho Marx is great, but you've got to be careful.'
Ajay names his action plan after Lenin's manifesto 'What is to be done'. Amit replies: 'with hindsight we know is what is not to be done.'

C.L.R. James's 'What do they know of cricket, who only cricket know', which Amit notes was itself a riff on Rudyard Kipling's 'what do they know of Britain who only Britain know.' Amit ends with his own twist: 'what do they know of depth only depth know.'
Bob Dylan's line, cited by Amit for lifelong renewal: if you're not busy being born, you're busy dying.

Amit on Henry Ford and Elon Musk: transport people wanted a faster horse until Ford dreamed of cars, and 'it takes an Elon Musk to think of Mars. Now, however outlandish, and literally outlandish in this case, you think that is…'
Amit teasing Ajay: 'I know you have depth in eight subjects you are happy to talk about and eight more you will not reveal to the public.'
Amit on specialists: 'they'll get work done out of you for a while. After that, they'll get it done from AI.'
Ajay on the Swedish state: 'I mean you need to be a real ideologue to be irritated at Sweden. I confess I'm a soft pinko. I love Sweden.'

Ajay's second item under 'what is to be done': 'there is an obscure YouTube show by Amit Varma and Ajay Shah which is called Everything Is Everything.' The episode ends on the same joke, with Amit adding 'the YouTube shows that expand the discourse, how could you forget that?' and Ajay agreeing: 'to get to those three things, you need great YouTube shows.'

Ajay attacks the Swachh Bharat planners: 'What kind of water and sanitation person are you if you think that there'll be toilet but you haven't thought through how the water will come and how the sewage will go out?' Amit, defensively: 'This was not my decision.'
Amit plugging their 10.5-hour Seen and the Unseen episode: 'so if you haven't seen that yet, gentle readers, [it] is a lot for you to gently read.'
